title: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (1 of 7)
hook: a whole Upanishad that begins with a question a child might ask
tomorrow: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (2 of 7)

segments.voice: Last week, the whole Isha in eighteen verses: hiranmaya; uncover it, so I may see. All this pervaded by the Lord, and the face of truth covered with gold. Did you look past one golden lid? Day two hundred thirty-nine.

Small children ask the best questions, right up until we teach them to stop. Why is the sky blue? Where was I before I was born? And sometimes, lying in bed: who's thinking my thoughts? Most of us laughed that one off by age ten. This week's Upanishad doesn't. It opens with exactly that question, asked by a student to a teacher, and it takes it completely seriously. It's called the Kena, and like the Isha it's named after its first word. Kena means: by whom?
screen: `WHO'S THINKING MY THOUGHTS?` → `THE QUESTION WE STOP ASKING.` → `KENA: BY WHOM?`

segments.voice: Here is the first verse, the student's question. By whom willed, by whom sent, does the mind fly out to its objects? By whom commanded does the first breath move? By whom impelled do people speak this speech? And what god sets the eye and the ear to their work? Four questions. Mind, breath, speech, eye and ear. Notice what they have in common. They're the things you think of as you. Your thinking, your breathing, your talking, your seeing. And the question asks: who's behind them? What makes the mind go? Think about it for a second. You didn't decide to have your next thought. It just arrived. You don't usually decide to breathe; it breathes. Your ear hears the traffic whether you want it to or not. So who, or what, is doing the doing? The Kena comes from the Sama Veda, the Veda of chanted song, and it's short: four sections, a few dozen verses. The first two sections are the teacher's answer, in paradoxes. The last two sections tell a story: the gods win a battle, take the credit, and meet a mysterious being they can't recognize. That story is our word for the week, the story of the gods and Brahman, and we'll get to it on day four. But first the question has to land. Brahman, which you've met before, is the tradition's word for the ultimate reality, the ground of everything. The Kena is going to say that Brahman is the answer to by whom. Not a thing the mind can grab. The one the mind runs on.
screen: `KENA: BY WHOM?` · `WHO SENDS THE MIND OUT?` · `MIND, BREATH, SPEECH, EYE, EAR.` · `THE ONE THE MIND RUNS ON.` · then, large: `WHO IMPELS THE MIND?`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Sit, close your eyes, and just watch for the next thought. Don't make one. Wait for it. When it comes, notice: you didn't order it. It arrived. Then watch for the next one. Between them, if there's a gap, rest there. You can gently ask the Kena's question, not to answer it, just to hold it: by whom? Then go back to watching. The bell holds the time.
Kena, by whom? The question that opens this Upanishad: by whom does the mind fly out to its objects, by whom does the first breath move?
Your line: the one behind the ear. Today, once, when you hear a sound, ask what's doing the hearing. Day two hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: The Kena Upanishad is studied in Hindu Vedanta traditions as a short, central text; its opening question, 'kena?', by whom?, is often used as a starting point for self-inquiry.

original.note: Sanskrit: kena, by whom?; the Upanishad's first word and its name.

trapdoor: what you thought: I think my thoughts, and that's the end of it.

what a scholar hears: the Kena is also called the Talavakara Upanishad, after the Talavakara (Jaiminiya) Brahmana of the Sama Veda it belongs to.
